title: Circulatory System
tagline: Blood and lymph, the heart and its double circulation, blood vessels, pulse and blood pressure.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: The human circulatory system is a closed transport network: a muscular double pump drives blood through arteries, capillaries and veins, while lymph drains leaked tissue fluid back into the bloodstream. Blood carries oxygen from lungs, nutrients from the gut, hormones from glands and wastes to the kidneys, while defending the body with leucocytes and clotting platelets. This chapter covers the composition and functions of blood, the structure of the heart and the pathway of double circulation, the differences between arteries, veins and capillaries, and the clinical measurements of pulse and blood pressure.

facts.label: Blood volume
facts.value: About 5 litres in an adult; plasma ~55%, cells ~45%

facts.label: Double circulation
facts.value: Pulmonary circuit (right heart ↔ lungs) and systemic circuit (left heart ↔ body)

facts.label: Normal BP
facts.value: About 120/80 mm Hg; 140/90 or above treated as hypertension

blocks.text: Blood is a fluid connective tissue with about 45% formed elements suspended in 55% plasma. Erythrocytes (red blood cells) are biconcave, enucleate discs packed with haemoglobin, whose iron binds oxygen reversibly and gives blood its colour; their shape maximises surface area for diffusion. Leucocytes (white blood cells) are nucleated and defend the body: granulocytes such as neutrophils engulf bacteria, while agranulocytes such as lymphocytes produce antibodies and provide immunity. Platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments that initiate clotting: when a vessel is damaged they stick to the injury site and trigger a cascade converting fibrinogen to fibrin, whose mesh traps blood cells and seals the wound. Plasma is ~90% water carrying dissolved nutrients, wastes, salts and plasma proteins such as fibrinogen and albumin. Lymph is tissue fluid drained by lymph capillaries: it carries fats absorbed from the intestine, recycles proteins and returns fluid to the blood near the heart, while passing through lymph nodes where pathogens are destroyed.

items.meaning: Red blood cell; biconcave, enucleate, carries haemoglobin.
White blood cell; nucleated; defends against pathogens.
Cell fragment that initiates blood clotting.
Liquid portion of blood carrying dissolved substances.
Tissue fluid in lymph vessels; returns protein-rich fluid to blood and carries absorbed fats.
Insoluble protein mesh forming the clot framework.

items: RBCs: no nucleus (more room for haemoglobin), ~120-day lifespan, made in red bone marrow.
Haemoglobin binds O2 in lungs (oxyhaemoglobin) and releases it in tissues.
WBCs: neutrophils phagocytose bacteria; lymphocytes make antibodies; both are nucleated.
Platelets + clotting factors -> fibrinogen -> fibrin mesh -> clot; clot retraction pulls wound edges together.
Plasma proteins: fibrinogen (clotting), albumin (osmotic balance), antibodies (immunity).
Lymph nodes filter lymph and destroy pathogens with lymphocytes; swelling signals infection.

items.text: A cut stops bleeding within minutes even without a bandage — platelet plug plus fibrin mesh.
items.note: Haemophilia is genetic inability to clot properly; carriers bleed excessively from minor injuries.

items.text: Swollen glands in the neck during infection are enlarged lymph nodes full of working lymphocytes.
items.note: The swelling is the immune system actively multiplying its defenders.

learn.title: Heart, double circulation and blood vessels

blocks.text: The human heart is a four-chambered muscular pump between the lungs. Deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the vena cava into the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns via the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, passes the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, and is pumped through the aorta to the whole body. The left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall because it must generate pressure for systemic circulation, while the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. Because blood passes the heart twice per circuit, this is double circulation: it keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely separate and maintains high pressure to the body, supporting the high metabolic rate of mammals. Valves in the heart and in veins ensure one-way flow. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure with thick elastic walls; veins return it at low pressure with thinner walls, valves and surrounding-muscle assistance; capillaries are one-cell-thick vessels where exchange of substances actually occurs.

items: Double circulation = pulmonary circuit + systemic circuit; blood passes the heart twice.
Advantages: complete separation of oxygenated/deoxygenated blood; sustained high systemic pressure for endothermy.
Left ventricle wall thickest — it powers the systemic circuit.
Arteries: thick elastic walls, carry blood AWAY from heart (pulmonary artery is the deoxygenated exception).
Veins: thin walls, valves, low pressure; skeletal-muscle contraction helps return blood from limbs.
Capillaries: walls one cell thick; huge total cross-section slows flow for exchange at tissues.

items.text: Standing for long causes ankle swelling — venous pooling; walking squeezes leg muscles and pumps blood back.
items.note: This is why vein valves and muscle pumps matter against gravity.

items.text: The pulmonary artery is an artery carrying deoxygenated blood — arteries are defined by direction, not oxygenation.
items.note: A classic exam trap; the pulmonary vein likewise carries oxygenated blood.

items.meaning: Two circuits — pulmonary and systemic — per single heart beat cycle.
Main artery carrying oxygenated blood from left ventricle to the body.
Large vein returning deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
Right heart to lungs and back — to load oxygen and unload CO2.

blocks.text: Each ventricular contraction sends a wave of distension along the arteries; this is the pulse, felt wherever an artery runs near the surface — the radial artery at the wrist is standard. Pulse rate equals heart rate, about 72 per minute at rest, rising with exercise, emotion or fever as the nervous and hormonal systems increase cardiac output. Blood pressure is the lateral pressure blood exerts on arterial walls, measured with a sphygmomanometer and reported as two figures: systolic pressure (~120 mm Hg) during ventricular contraction, and diastolic pressure (~80 mm Hg) during ventricular relaxation, when the aortic valve closes and elastic recoil maintains flow. Persistent pressure at or above 140/90 mm Hg is hypertension, which strains the heart and damages vessel walls, accelerating atherosclerosis; low pressure may indicate shock or haemorrhage. Regular exercise, low salt intake and avoiding smoking keep pressure in the healthy range.

items: Pulse: wave of artery wall expansion with each ventricular systole; felt at radial, carotid, temporal arteries.
Resting pulse ~60–80/min; trained athletes lower; exercise raises both rate and stroke volume.
Systolic ~120 mm Hg (contraction); diastolic ~80 mm Hg (relaxation); written 120/80.
Hypertension ≥ 140/90 — 'silent killer' because it usually has no symptoms.
Sphygmomanometer + stethoscope detect Korotkoff sounds at systolic and their disappearance at diastolic.
Heart sounds (lub-dub) come from valve closure, not from blood flow itself.

items.text: After running, both pulse rate and blood pressure rise — the body demands more oxygen per minute.
items.note: Diastolic pressure changes little; systolic rises with cardiac output.

items.text: 'Lub' = AV valves closing at start of systole; 'dub' = semilunar valves closing at start of diastole.
items.note: Valve closure order explains the two sounds — a favourite short-answer question.

keyPoints: Blood = plasma (55%) + cells (45%): RBCs carry oxygen, WBCs defend, platelets clot.
RBCs are enucleate biconcave discs full of haemoglobin.
Lymph returns tissue fluid and absorbed fats to the blood and filters pathogens in nodes.
Heart has four chambers; AV and semilunar valves enforce one-way flow.
Double circulation = pulmonary + systemic; complete separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Left ventricle has the thickest wall because it powers systemic circulation.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; veins return it with valves at low pressure.
Capillaries are the site of exchange — one-cell-thick walls.
Pulse = arterial wave with each systole; normal ~72/min.
experimentFocus: Pulse measurement: count radial pulse for 15 s ×4 at rest, then immediately after exercise, then at 1-minute intervals — expect recovery toward baseline.
Know the definitions inside out: arteries leave the heart, veins return it — oxygenation is NOT the defining feature.
Heart sound questions: name the valve closing, the phase, and which heart sound results.
examFocus: Labelled heart diagrams must show all four chambers, four main vessels, and both valve types — practice the labels.
Double circulation advantages: separate blood + sustained high pressure; stating only 'cleaner blood' loses marks.
Why is the left ventricle wall thicker? Answer in terms of pressure needed for the systemic circuit.
BP questions expect both figures defined and the hypertension threshold given.

vocabulary.meaning: Iron-containing pigment in RBCs that reversibly binds oxygen.
Protein mesh forming the clot in coagulation.
Tissue fluid drained by lymphatics; carries fats and filters through nodes.
Contraction phase of the heart, producing peak arterial pressure.
Relaxation phase, with baseline elastic-recoil pressure.
Persistently high blood pressure (≥140/90 mm Hg).

questions.explanation: Lymphocytes are agranular leucocytes that produce antibodies specific to antigens; neutrophils act by phagocytosis instead.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing neutrophils — they engulf bacteria directly but do not make antibodies.

questions.prompt: Which structure has the thickest muscular wall?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps blood through the whole systemic circuit against high resistance, so its wall is the thickest.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the right ventricle because it 'pumps harder' — it only reaches the nearby lungs.

questions.prompt: A blood vessel carrying deoxygenated blood is:
questions.explanation: Arteries are defined by carrying blood AWAY from the heart; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming all arteries carry oxygenated blood — direction from the heart is the definition.

questions.prompt: Exchange of substances between blood and tissues occurs mainly in the:
questions.explanation: Capillaries have walls one cell thick and a huge total cross-section slowing the flow, ideal for diffusion.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing arteries because blood moves fastest there — fast flow is least suited to exchange.

questions.prompt: The normal blood pressure of a healthy adult is approximately:
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is quoted systolic first (contraction) then diastolic (relaxation); 140/90 is the hypertension threshold.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 80/120 — the convention is systolic first because it is the higher, contraction-phase figure.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the liquid portion of blood is called ________, and the insoluble protein that forms the framework of a blood clot is ________.
questions.explanation: Plasma carries dissolved substances; during clotting fibrinogen is converted to insoluble fibrin whose mesh traps cells.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing fibrinogen (soluble, in plasma) with fibrin (insoluble, in the clot).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium through the ________ and oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium through the ________.
questions.explanation: The vena cava returns body blood; the pulmonary veins return blood oxygenated in the lungs to the left atrium.
questions.commonMistake: Saying pulmonary artery for the return path — arteries always leave the heart.

questions.prompt: State the functions of blood under three headings: transport, defence and clotting.
questions.answer: Transport: red blood cells carry oxygen as oxyhaemoglobin from lungs to tissues and carbon dioxide back; plasma carries nutrients from the intestine, wastes to the kidneys, hormones from glands and heat. Defence: white blood cells — neutrophils and monocytes engulf and digest bacteria by phagocytosis, while lymphocytes produce antibodies that neutralise antigens; lymph nodes filter pathogens from lymph. Clotting: platelets collect at a wound and release factors that convert fibrinogen into fibrin; the fibrin mesh traps blood cells to form a clot, preventing blood loss and sealing the body against infection.
questions.explanation: Three clear categories with named cells and molecules earn full marks; loose 'it protects us' loses most of them.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting plasma's role in transport — RBCs alone are not the whole transport answer.

questions.prompt: Trace the path of a drop of blood from the right atrium to the left ventricle, naming the valves it passes.
questions.answer: Right atrium -> through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle -> right ventricle contracts, blood passes the pulmonary (semilunar) valve into the pulmonary artery -> travels to the lungs where it gives up carbon dioxide and takes up oxygen -> returns oxygenated blood through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium -> through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle.
questions.explanation: The path is the pulmonary circuit; each valve must be named in the correct order along with the vessel changes.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting the valves entirely — the question explicitly asks for them, and they carry the marks.

questions.prompt: What is double circulation? State two advantages, and explain how the structure of the heart is adapted to it.
questions.answer: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: the pulmonary circuit (right heart to lungs and back) and the systemic circuit (left heart to body and back). Advantages: (1) oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept completely separate, so tissues receive blood with the maximum oxygen concentration; (2) blood reaching the body has just been pumped at high pressure from the heart, maintaining the rapid flow and high metabolic rate needed by warm-blooded mammals. Structural adaptations: the heart has four separate chambers preventing mixing; the left ventricle has a much thicker muscular wall to generate the higher pressure of the systemic circuit; the right ventricle has a thinner wall suited to the short, low-resistance pulmonary circuit; and valves ensure unidirectional flow in each pass.
questions.explanation: Definition, two advantages, and three structural adaptations with reasoning — that is the full-marks shape for this classic 4-mark question.
questions.commonMistake: Listing chamber separation twice as two advantages — the second advantage must be about pressure/flow.

questions.prompt: A person's blood pressure is recorded as 150/95 mm Hg. What does each figure represent, what condition does this indicate, and name two lifestyle measures that would help.
questions.answer: 150 is the systolic pressure — the peak lateral pressure on artery walls when the ventricles contract. 95 is the diastolic pressure — the pressure remaining when the ventricles relax and the elastic arteries recoil. Both figures exceed the normal 120/80 and the hypertension threshold of 140/90, so this indicates hypertension, which strains the heart and damages arteries, raising the risk of atherosclerosis and stroke. Lifestyle measures: regular aerobic exercise to improve cardiac efficiency and lower pressure; reducing salt intake to reduce water retention and blood volume; also stopping smoking and managing weight.
questions.explanation: Each figure defined, the threshold quoted, and named measures — the applied-style answer examiners reward.
questions.commonMistake: Saying 'high blood pressure' without naming hypertension or quoting figures — definition marks are available and often missed.
